newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Implats sees little excitement in yr ahead.
newsitem.headline: Implats sees little excitement in yr ahead.

text.p: South Africa's Impala Platinum Holdings Ltd said on Tuesday it did not see an exciting year ahead although the declining rand might provide some relief to the company when it reports full year results.

Implats Managing Director Steve Kearney said at the results presentation for the six months to end-December 1996 that the 3.4 percent increase in attributable income to 96 million rand was satisfactory.
But he did not see exciting results ahead for the rest of the financial year.
"Although the rand will provide some relief for us... it is unlikely that the first half will be matched by the second half," Kearney said.

He said the company was gearing for better days in the medium to longer term and had prepared a new vision for Implats as a result of the European Commission halting its merger with the platinum interests of Lonrho Plc.
The EU last April blocked the move because it was seen as anti-trust with the planned new company set to hold 28 percent of the world's platinum market.
Kearney said Implats now believed it had the best efficiency levels in the platinum industry.
"We have come a long way from being the worst in the industry five years ago to what we believe now is the best," he said.
The company's new vision envisages measures to lower working costs but advances in the second half would not be enough to compensate for projected weak metal prices.
Implats said its board had agreed to the 398 million rand capital expenditure No 1 vertical shaft decline extension project.

The project will replace 20 percent of Impala's current production and will be a first step in plan to maintain output of 1.0 million ounces a year while pushing back by 15 years the need to develop a capital intensive vertical shaft system from the surface.

The project, which would see completion around the turn of the century, would involve greater use of modern technology -- including the use of a mono-rail system to haul ore and bring miners to the surface from a depth of about 1,300 metres.
"In order to mine this efficiently, we will bring in new technology," Implats senior consulting engineer operations, John Smithies said at the results presentation.
